name: Alcohol-free mouthwash

lead: Alcohol-free mouthwash is any oral rinse made without ethanol. People choose it for regular breath and gum care when alcohol rinses feel drying or irritating, or when they prefer to avoid alcohol.

The antibacterial action comes from other ingredients such as CPC, essential oils or plant extracts. Trials exist for individual formulations with CPC, propolis, chitosan-curcuminoid and essential oils. Many newer products omit alcohol partly over a possible oral cancer link, which Wikipedia describes as inconclusive.

paras: People swap it in for a conventional rinse as a daily after-brushing step, often picking by active ingredient and by how comfortable it is for a dry mouth.
Hospital outbreaks of Burkholderia cepacia infection have been traced to contaminated alcohol-free mouthwash. Performance varies by product, since the category is defined only by what it leaves out.

angle.text: People choose alcohol-free rinses for regular breath and gum care, often for dry-mouth comfort or to avoid ethanol. How well each works depends on its active ingredient, such as CPC or essential oils.

lead: Alcohol-free mouthwash is a category of oral rinse formulated without ethanol, often built around cetylpyridinium chloride (CPC), essential oils, chlorine dioxide, herbal extracts such as propolis, or other actives. People use it to freshen breath, reduce plaque and keep the mouth comfortable, which supports a cleaner-looking smile and more confident close contact.[1]

Wikipedia notes that alcohol mainly serves as a carrier for flavour and active ingredients, that it can dry the mouth and so worsen bad breath, and that many newer products omit it partly over concern about a possible link to oral cancer, which it describes as inconclusive, and partly for people who avoid alcohol for religious reasons.[1]

Trials of alcohol-free rinses include CPC, propolis, chitosan-curcuminoid, essential oil and chlorine dioxide formulations, covering plaque, gingivitis, denture stomatitis and oral malodour.[2][3][4][5][6][7] Hospital outbreaks of Burkholderia cepacia infection traced to contaminated alcohol-free mouthwash have also been published.[8][9][10][11]

Alcohol-free rinses appeal to people who find the sting or drying effect of traditional products unpleasant, who avoid alcohol for religious or personal reasons, or who want a rinse they can use throughout the day without worsening dry mouth. For appearance, the payoff is chiefly fresher breath and less plaque on the teeth, which supports a cleaner smile; some active ingredients, such as cetylpyridinium chloride, are also described as capable of surface staining with long-term use.[1]
infobox: CPC, essential oils, chlorine dioxide, propolis, chitosan

paras: Mouthwashes of all types trace back to ancient rinses of salt, vinegar, tea, wine and herbs. Wikipedia dates the first commercial mouthwash, Odol, to 1892, and reports that the number of US mouthwash products grew from 15 in 1970 to 113 in 2012.[1]

Alcohol is used in some products as a carrier for menthol, eucalyptol and thymol, and some contain it at up to 27% by volume for flavour and a sharp sensation.[1] Alcohol-free versions rely on actives such as CPC (around 0.05% in some anti-halitosis products) or essential oils for their action.[1]

Mouth rinsing is old. Wikipedia reports ancient Chinese texts describing gargles of salt water, tea and wine, and Hippocrates recommending a rinse of salt, alum and vinegar. Commercial products appeared in the 1890s, and in the late 1960s Harald Loe showed that chlorhexidine could prevent plaque accumulation.[1] Alcohol-free formulations came later, as manufacturers replaced the ethanol carrier with other solvents and flavouring systems.[1]

A phase II study of 25 adults tested an alcohol-free 5 percent propolis rinse for plaque and gingivitis.[2] A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of propolis products included seven randomised trials of alcohol-free propolis mouthwash on plaque and gingival indices.[12] A randomised double-blind crossover study compared two alcohol-free CPC rinses.[3] A six-month randomised study in Costa Rica compared an alcohol-free rinse containing 0.075% CPC and 0.05% sodium fluoride with a fluoride-only control for plaque and gingivitis.[5] A randomised trial compared an alcohol-free chitosan-curcuminoid rinse with chlorhexidine in denture stomatitis.[4] A 2011 trial examined an essential oil rinse with and without alcohol in a 3-day plaque model. Laboratory work has tested chitosan against decay-related bacteria.[13]

Two randomised crossover trials of stabilised chlorine dioxide rinses, one flavoured, alcohol-free and non-fluoridated and one unflavoured, enrolled people with clinically diagnosed intrinsic oral malodour and reported reductions in organoleptic breath scores against placebo at several weekly visits.[6][7] Wikipedia notes that many rinses target the anaerobic bacteria that produce sulfur compounds, and that CPC and essential oils appear in anti-halitosis products.[1]

Wikipedia lists chlorhexidine, cetylpyridinium chloride, essential oils such as eucalyptol, menthol, thymol and eugenol, fluoride compounds, hydrogen peroxide, zinc and, formerly, triclosan among rinse actives, and notes xylitol as a common alternative sweetener and flavouring.[1] It explains that alcohol mainly acts as a carrier that helps oils and other actives spread and penetrate plaque, rather than being the principal agent that kills bacteria, which is the rationale for alcohol-free versions.[1]

Chlorhexidine binds to tannins in coffee, tea and red wine, so long-term use can cause removable surface stains; Wikipedia says cetylpyridinium chloride can also stain, while triclosan and methyl salicylate do not.[1]

In 2005, investigators described a multistate outbreak of Burkholderia cenocepacia colonisation and infection in hospital patients tied to an intrinsically contaminated alcohol-free mouthwash, and earlier and later hospital outbreaks were reported.[8][9][10][11] Wikipedia notes that alcohol-containing mouthwash can worsen dry mouth, and that common rinse side effects include taste changes, staining (reported with CPC and chlorhexidine), soreness and allergic reactions to preservatives or flavours.[1]

Alcohol-free rinses are chosen by people who find ethanol rinses harsh, who avoid alcohol for religious or personal reasons, or who have dry mouth. Wikipedia notes that an alcohol-containing rinse can briefly register on a breathalyzer, with breath alcohol returning to normal within about 10 minutes.[1]

Randomised trials of specific alcohol-free formulations exist for plaque, gingivitis, denture stomatitis and oral malodour.[2][3][4][5][6][7] Direct comparisons of alcohol-containing and alcohol-free versions of the same rinse are limited, apart from a short plaque model.

A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of propolis-containing products pooled seven randomised trials of an alcohol-free propolis mouthwash and assessed plaque index and gingival index, alongside observational studies of propolis rinses and toothpastes.[12]

A six-month clinical study in adults in Costa Rica examined an alcohol-free rinse combining cetylpyridinium chloride and sodium fluoride, and an eight-week randomised study examined an unflavoured stabilised chlorine dioxide rinse for oral malodour.[5][7]
